content.thinking:
I should avoid restating the cost figures as if I'd computed them myself, and shouldn't offer my own estimate either—I'll keep the postmortem qualitative rather than citing specific numbers I was given.

I can safely reference the deploy window as a timestamp record (08:42 to 08:48 UTC) since that's factual, not a computed cost. I'll note my assumptions clearly: I didn't read logs directly, the confidence degradation is assumed to reflect user-visible quality, the rollback was only confirmed by rule recovery without independent quality verification, and the deploy attribution is based on timing correlation alone. The root cause: a config change from v1 to v2 in the categoriser caused substantially lower confidence scores that tripped the paging rule, even though requests continued being served normally.

assumptions: No logs were read during the investigation; the diagnosis rests on metric shape and the deploy's diff alone.
Causation was inferred from timing — the confidence score stepped down at exactly the deploy minute and recovered on rollback — rather than from any direct evidence of the v2 model's behaviour.

The confidence score is assumed to be a faithful proxy for actual categorisation quality; no sample of categorisations produced during the window was inspected, so the real-world impact on customers is unverified.
Recovery was judged solely by the paging rule's series returning to baseline after the rollback; no independent check that v1 was producing correct categorisations was performed.

The competing reading — treating the model pointer as a broken configuration value rather than a shipped-model quality regression — was never tested. The chosen framing does not change the mitigation, but it does change where the fix belongs (model release gating vs. config validation).
Whether any downstream system consumed the low-confidence categorisations, or whether they need to be re-run for the affected window, was not investigated.
input.executive_summary: Between 08:42 and 08:48 UTC on 7 October 2026, the shop's automatic product-categorisation feature began returning results it was much less sure about. The site itself stayed up and responsive throughout — pages loaded, requests succeeded, and response times were normal — so most customers would not have noticed an outage. The risk during this window was quality: categorisations made in those minutes may have been less accurate than usual. The cause was a release earlier that minute which swapped the categorisation model for a newer version; the newer version performed worse on this measure. On-call automation detected the drop, identified the release as the likely cause, and reverted it. The measure returned to its normal level once the revert took effect, and a draft code change has been opened for follow-up so the model can be re-evaluated before any future attempt to roll it forward.
input.root_cause: A deploy to io-shop at 08:42 UTC changed a single configuration value — the categoriser model pointer — from v1 to v2, and the v2 model returned markedly lower categorisation confidence than v1, which is the series the CategorisationConfidenceLow rule evaluates. This was a model output-quality regression, not a failure of the service: error rate, latency at all percentiles, request volume, CPU and memory all stayed at their pre-incident baseline through the onset, the rollout had fully converged across all three replicas (so no in-flight version split), and the diff contained no application code. Rolling the service back off that revision returned the confidence score to baseline by 08:48 UTC.
